Celebrities often face enormous pressure to maintain a polished public image because their reputation is closely tied to their professional success. As Pipe Dream explains, their appearance, behavior, and personal lives are constantly scrutinized, making even minor mistakes or seemingly harmless comments potential sources of public criticism.
Endorsement deals, acting opportunities, brand partnerships, and fan loyalty can all depend on how marketable a celebrity appears. This creates an environment in which public figures must think carefully about what they reveal, how they behave, and how their words might be interpreted by audiences.
The constant attention from paparazzi, tabloids, interviews, and online audiences makes it particularly difficult for celebrities to separate their professional identities from their private lives. Even their clothing choices, relationships, parenting decisions, and casual remarks can become subjects of widespread discussion.
Fans may also expect their favorite stars to be attractive, successful, inspiring, and morally consistent, placing unrealistic demands on people who are still human and capable of making mistakes.
Trying to meet these expectations can contribute to stress, anxiety , and burnout, while some celebrities may begin to feel disconnected from their authentic identities after spending so much time maintaining a public persona. As a result, being candid can come with considerable risks, especially when a single unexpected revelation could lead to unwanted headlines or criticism.
One reason audiences become so invested in these revelations is the emotional connection they develop with famous people. According to the American Psychological Association , this can happen through parasocial relationships, which are one-sided emotional bonds in which people feel as though they know a public figure personally, despite never having met them.
Repeated exposure to interviews, videos, livestreams, and personal stories makes a celebrity's personality, opinions, and sense of humor increasingly familiar. Social media can strengthen this feeling by creating the impression of direct interaction through likes, comments, replies, and behind-the-scenes content.
Consequently, fans may feel unusually connected to celebrities whose lives they follow closely, even though the relationship exists entirely from their side.

items.desc: Thanksgiving is almost here, and the internet is already serving up plenty of laughs! These funny memes capture the holiday mood perfectly and might even put you in the festive spirit. Grab a snack, Pandas, and get ready for a good chuckle!
items.text:
The story behind Thanksgiving begins in 1620, when a ship called the Mayflower arrived in what is now Massachusetts, carrying 102 English passengers hoping to establish a settlement. The group included religious separatists who wanted to practice their faith freely, along with other passengers looking for a new start.
Their first winter was brutal. Food was scarce, illness spread, and many settlers passed before spring arrived. By the following autumn, the survivors had grown enough food for a harvest celebration.
The settlers didn't get through those difficult early months entirely on their own. The Wampanoag people had lived in the region for generations, and their leader, Ousamequin, also known as Massasoit, eventually allied with the English.
The Wampanoag shared their knowledge of local crops and helped the settlers learn how to grow food in the unfamiliar environment. In autumn 1621, after the English had gathered their first successful harvest, a group of Wampanoag men joined them for a celebration .
The celebration lasted three days, and we have a description from English settler Edward Winslow , who wrote about the gathering in a letter later published in 1622. He explained that the governor had sent four men out to hunt birds, and they brought back enough to feed the settlement for almost a week.
The Wampanoag visitors also went hunting and brought five deer to the gathering. They also practiced shooting and did other activities, so it wasn't just three days of sitting around a table eating. Interestingly, this event wasn't called Thanksgiving at the time, and it wasn't repeated every year as an annual holiday. The name and the familiar traditions came much later.
It took more than 200 years for Thanksgiving to become a national holiday. One woman who helped make that happen was Sarah Josepha Hale , an editor and writer best known for writing "Mary Had a Little Lamb."
Starting in 1827, she campaigned for a nationwide Thanksgiving celebration , writing articles and sending letters to presidents for decades. Her efforts finally paid off in 1863, when President Abraham Lincoln issued a proclamation declaring the last Thursday of November a national day of Thanksgiving.
The country was in the middle of the Civil War, and Lincoln hoped the occasion would encourage people to reflect and pray for peace.

items.text:
Japanese artist Ayumi Tsuchiya creates playful, interactive sculptures and installations that explore sound and movement. From a chair that opens and closes like a flower to a series of giant wooden cogs that play music, each piece encourages childlike curiosity and exploration.
In 2008, Tsuchiya chose to leave her corporate job to study spatial design at Tama Art University, where she began developing her whimsical ideas. Today, her handcrafted works are exhibited in museums, science centers, and art events, and she collaborates with companies including MUJI , Karimoku, Benesse, and Tokyo Disney Resort.
Tsuchiya is largely self-taught in woodworking, making her imaginative, tactile work even more impressive. Her Thumbelina Chair, designed in 2019, invites you to experience the world from the perspective of the tiny character it takes its name from. As you sit down, its wooden “petals” gently fold around you, creating a cozy, cocoon-like enclosure.
Another standout piece is the Gear Music Box , a giant, interactive wooden instrument operated by turning a hand crank. Each oversized wooden gear is tuned to a different note. As you turn the hand crank, the gears rotate, and the wooden balls placed between their teeth strike the mechanisms to produce sound. By moving the balls into different positions, you can change the note sequence and compose your own melodies.
Over time, Tsuchiya noticed a fascinating difference between how kids and adults approach her work. While children tend to engage with it instinctively, adults are often more cautious. “Children are geniuses,” says Tsuchiya. “That’s not to say adults aren’t—it’s just that because they understand the rules of society and try to live by common sense, they seek an explanation first. Through my work, I hope that adults, in particular, will reconnect with the sensibility that lies dormant within them.”

items.text:
When artists get together, ideas will inevitably flow. They discuss inspiration, leading to new ways of thinking and experimentation. Sometimes, artists will produce their work separately but on the same overarching subject. It’s fascinating to watch a theme unfold through different lenses. One exhibition looks at how friendship, artistic exchange, and shared summers influenced the work of three American artists: Milton Avery (1885–1965), Adolph Gottlieb (1903–1974), and Mark Rothko (1903–1970). Now on view at The Phillips Collection , Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea features about 90 paintings, watercolors, drawings, and sketches the three developed over 40 years.
The artists met in New York City but traveled to Cape Ann in Gloucester, Mass., to spend summers there beginning in the 1930s. Avery first visited the area in the 1920s, before introducing Gottlieb and Rothko to the coastline. While there, they spent the summer drawing, painting, and exchanging ideas. In having this time to “live like an artist,” as Avery’s wife Sally Michel Avery, also an artist, described, the site became a foundation for experimentation and discovery.
Each artist had their own way of working. Avery was known for his representational art, while Gottlieb and Rothko became internationally recognized for abstract art. But even with different sensibilities, the exhibition shows how Cape Ann, along with expressive use of color and experimentation with scale, fostered each artist’s development. For Avery, this meant harbor sketches and coastal scenes; for Rothko, it included “color-drenched canvases”; and for Gottlieb, it meant beach box motifs, which would eventually lead to Pictographs .
“Exploring the friendship and shared experiences of Avery, Gottlieb, and Rothko during their summers on Cape Ann offers a fresh perspective on their artistic development,” explains Renée Maurer, associate curator at The Phillips Collection and the exhibition’s coordinating curator. “This story will be new to many of our guests, and several of the works have never been on public view. Bringing together the artists in this context has allowed us to look closely at the exchanges that shaped their work as they responded to influences and new directions in American modernism.”

items.text:
“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) by Vincent van Gogh , 1890. (Photo: courtesy of Sotheby’s)
A painting by Vincent van Gogh has sold for a record-breaking $190.4 million at Sotheby’s in New York, making it the most expensive work by the artist to ever sell at auction. The painting, titled Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees) , was completed just two months before Van Gogh’s death in 1890. However, in the days leading up to the auction, the painting became the subject of a dispute surrounding its ownership during the Nazi era.
Van Gogh painted Blossoming Chestnut Trees on May 24, 1890, just days after arriving in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise following his stay at a psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The painting depicts people walking along a street lined with blossoming chestnut trees, which Van Gogh captured using his signature bold brushstrokes and vibrant colors. Despite being one of the last works he ever completed, the painting had been held in a private collection for decades.
The piece belonged to the Argentine Blaquier-Arrieta family since 1975, but its ownership history goes back much further. In 1909, the painting was purchased by Samuel Fischer, a prominent German Jewish publisher. Following his death in 1934, the painting remained in the family until it was sold in 1936, during a period of increasing Nazi persecution of Jewish people in Germany.
Just days before the painting was set to go to auction, descendants of Fischer and his wife, Hedwig, called for the sale to be postponed. The family raised concerns about the circumstances surrounding the painting’s sale in 1936, questioning whether their relatives had been forced to part with it due to Nazi persecution.
However, just one day before the auction, Sotheby’s announced that the Fischer descendants and the painting’s current owners had reached an agreement, allowing the sale to move forward. While the details of the agreement have not been made public, the Fischer family expressed their appreciation for the discussions and for the acknowledgment of their family’s suffering during the Holocaust.
The painting ultimately sold for $165 million, with auction fees bringing the total to $190.4 million. This surpassed the previous auction record for a Van Gogh painting, which was set in 2022 when Verger avec cyprès ( Orchard with Cypresses ) sold for $117.2 million at Christie’s.

items.text:
An Arizona community is celebrating a local grandfather who found a missing toddler in the middle of the cold desert night.
Honored by the sheriff’s office as an outstanding citizen, Jay Stewart said he felt what everyone else who was searching felt, saying “she may not be our child, but she could be.”
The story begins at sundown on November 17th, when, playing with her siblings, 2-year-old Vella Campillo wandered off into the desert surrounding the city of Eloy, wearing nothing but a diaper.
Vella’s parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, contacted police shortly after 5 p.m., saying that she was being looked after by another family member but had gone missing. Any parent can relate: one moment a child is there; the next they’re gone.
Pinal County Sheriff’s Office and local volunteers began to scour the area as night closed in and temperatures began to fall. Among them was father and grandfather Jay Stewart.
“The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child,” Stewart told local news. “I can’t imagine what they were going through.” He added that everyone he met was searching for Vella “for the same reason.”
“We loved her and wanted her back—she may not be our child, but she could be.”
Over the next 7 hours, Stewart, along with his fellow volunteers dozens of members from various law enforcement agencies, searched with flashlights amid 50°F temperatures. Drones and a helicopter were involved in the search, but the child’s miniature heat signature rendered the thermal imaging cameras ineffective.
The breakthrough came just after midnight when Stewart was investigating a line of bushes near a ditch where, unbeknownst to him, little Vella lay curled up. He would later call the Sheriff’s office to signal he’d found the girl, who was taken to the hospital after no small amount of convincing, latched as she was onto Stewart with no desire to let go.
She was reunited with her family shortly after with no injuries or hypothermia.

items.text:
For artist Sara Silks , the natural world has always sparked curiosity and inspiration. Growing up exploring the woods and waterways of the Ozarks in the Midwestern United States, she developed a deep connection to the landscape. Today, that familiarity informs her growing concern over the environmental changes taking place around her.
Her series Warming Effects explores these changes through layered photographic compositions that combine images of extreme weather with geometric shapes and intricate patterns. Photographs of ice, fire, storms, and other natural phenomena become the foundation for abstract arrangements that explore the tension between nature’s visual beauty and the uncertainty of a changing climate.
Silks approaches photography as an experimental process, drawing on her background in drawing and printmaking to move beyond traditional documentation. She prints her compositions on handmade Unryu washi paper and applies a labor-intensive cold wax finish, giving each work a distinctive tactile surface.
My Modern Met had the chance to speak with Silks about the inspiration behind Warming Effects , her intuitive approach to image-making, and how she uses photography to navigate her concerns about the environment. Read on for our exclusive interview with the artist.
How has your lifelong relationship with the Ozark landscape shaped the way you photograph it, particularly as climate change alters the natural world you know?
My relationship with the Ozarks began long before I thought of photographing it. As a child, I spent endless summer days exploring the hilly woods and lake water, often alone. I had the freedom to investigate whatever caught my attention. Those hours of discovery and quiet observation created a feeling of oneness with the landscape that has stayed with me throughout my life.
When I photograph it, those memories are present in what I notice and how I respond. Changes in a place so deeply familiar feel personal. My concern for the landscape grows out of that attachment and increasingly finds its way into the work.

While a little boy was fighting a deadly disease in the Children’s Hospital of New Orleans he longed for a place to go get some fresh air or distraction from his woes. Before he died, he and his family started a foundation to raise money—and five years later his wish was fulfilled.
Last week, his family celebrated the opening of the world’s first museum incorporated into a hospital—a fantastical ‘Imaginarium’ where sick kids and their families can go for art, movement, pretending, and fun.
Named after the nine-year-old, Walker Beery, Walker’s Imaginarium is a 15,000-square-foot children’s museum where patients can wander through rooms interacting with uniquely Louisiana themes: dancing to cajun music, exploring a bayou, joining a Mardi Gras parade, or enjoying a quiet moment among an animated fish tank.
Designed for a range of physical, sensory, and medical needs, kids in wheelchairs can play both mini-golf and foosball while rolling by the colorful ramps and murals—and forgetting they’re in a hospital. (See the video at the bottom…)
For the Beery family, Walker’s Imaginarium is a deeply personal expression of their son Walker’s vision to give back to others. In August 2019, he was diagnosed with pediatric brain cancer, yet through surgeries, hospital stays, and chemotherapy treatments, Walker’s infectious courage and grateful spirit always amazed his family and all who encountered him during his two-year battle at the hospital, recently renamed Manning Family Children’s.
Walker’s Imaginarium was funded entirely through philanthropic support and donations raised by the community and the lad’s foundation, Kids Join The Fight .
“Walker’s spirit is carried forward in the joy that is embedded in this amazing project,” said Walker’s dad Taylor, co-founder of Kids Join The Fight.
“Every child who finds a moment of escape, every family that experiences joy together carries Walker’s dream forward: to use his own experience to make someone else’s a little easier, and a little happier.”

items.text:
Millions of people with high blood pressure may be offered an actual cure for its root cause that would bring long-lasting relief.
Doctors were stunned by the latest study of patients who took the FDA-approved drug called baxdrostat, which showed that it reversed the condition—even for years after patients stopped taking the medication.
Baxdrostat (aka Baxfendy) is the first of a specific type of medication, known as extended aldosterone synthase inhibition (EASI), to hit the US market—although there are others, like lorundrostat, in the pipeline.
“Just under a quarter of the patients came off all treatment and had completely normal blood pressure,” Prof. Morris Brown, a hypertension specialist who led the study at Queen Mary University of London told The Guardian .
The treatment involves taking the new class of drugs for 6-12 months to target excess production of the hormone aldosterone, a common cause of high blood pressure. Unlike conventional treatments that control blood pressure, the EASI-treatment appears to reverse its underlying cause, removing the need for lifelong medication.
The findings raise the possibility that, for people with this type of high blood pressure—between 5 and 10% of hypertension cases—a cure is possible.
Previously, if your adrenal glands were producing too much aldosterone, it caused the kidneys to retain excess salt, raising your blood pressure—and the only cure was surgery to remove the entire gland.
The study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, followed 14 people treated at eight centers across the US. Researchers found that the EASI-treatment led to sustained reversal of excess aldosterone production and partial or complete resolution of high blood pressure for up to two years after treatment ended.
Hormone levels and blood pressure remained similar to, or lower than, those recorded during their treatment, suggesting that the benefits could persist long after people stop taking the drug.
The scientific basis for EASI-treatment dates back to a 2005 experiment in mice, which showed that deleting the gene responsible for producing aldosterone synthase caused the cells that make aldosterone to disappear. Researchers at Queen Mary predicted that prolonged treatment with an aldosterone synthase inhibitor might have a similar effect in humans, potentially removing the underlying cause of their hypertension.

items.title: Mysterious Mercury gets a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
items.desc: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
items.text:
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo has arrived at its final destination and is now in orbit around Mercury.
It‘s operating in an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.
"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.
"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.
So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit was a perilous one: a 37-minute handbrake turn that allowed it to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
The European Space Agency said on X that the probe had made contact and its telemetry data confirmed that it was now flying around the planet, though it's thrusters had fired for a shorter time than planned following a software issue.

A father-daughter entrepreneurial duo in India have pioneered a method of paper making with rhino dung harvested by locals.
Suddenly, they say, villagers who may come into conflict with rhino see them as a continual source of income, giving them a reason to protect these majestic beasts while also supporting their livelihoods.
Elrhino Stationery was co-founded by Mahesh Chandra Bora who first got the idea when he read about rhino dung paper making in Rajasthan, the scorching desert region in the west of the country.
If they could do it there, where hardly any rhino live, why not do it in Assam, home to some 2,900 greater one-horned rhinos?
The retired mining engineer got to work experimenting with production methods, knowing that the pulp to make the paper would come from the undigested plant fibers packed together in the animal’s dung balls.
The Better India writes that his first tests were done in the kitchen with his wife’s kitchen blender—no doubt endearing Chandra and the new venture to his beloved.
His daughter Nisha then left the corporate world where she had worked for 17 years to help, and in 2014 Elrhino was born.

The production process starts by trucking away rhino and elephant dung harvested by communities that live near the reserves where the animals thrive. Assam’s national parks contain some of the highest per-kilometer concentrations of rhino anywhere in the world, and protecting the animals is one of India’s great conservation success stories .

items.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
items.desc: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
items.text:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Typography affects how easily we can read text more than most people think. Some sans-serif fonts help us recognize letters quickly, while others can slow us down, especially when we only have a second to read.
This can make a real difference in daily life, like when you glance at a navigation screen while driving or check a notification on your phone. You may laugh, but comic sans is one of the most readable fonts available.

A clever visual concept loses its purpose when people cannot read the words that explain it. Even if someone reads the words correctly, it doesn’t always mean they understand a design the way it was meant.
Our brains are always sorting out what we see, picking out what stands out and what fades into the background. That’s why two people might look at the same image and notice totally different things.

Just shifting focus a little can change what someone sees.

Origami is usually associated with folding paper into intricate shapes, but researchers are now using the same basic idea to create structures big enough to walk beneath. A team led by MIT researchers has developed a new construction method inspired by origami that produces lightweight, rigid structures from flat sheets.
The technique builds on the work of artist and scientist Ron Resch , who began experimenting with repeating folded patterns, known as tessellations , in the 1960s. His designs showed how carefully placed folds could transform a flat sheet into complex three-dimensional surfaces.
“We are demonstrating structural origami on building scales,” says lead author Alfonso Parra Rubio, a graduate student at MIT’s Center for Bits and Atoms.
Instead of folding one enormous sheet, the researchers broke the idea into smaller pieces. Each triangular unit is folded individually, then connected to others to create a larger network of interwoven beams. Once assembled, the pieces lock together to form a strong structure without needing interior support columns.
This modular approach also makes the structures easier to build. The pieces can be cut from flat sheets of material, such as aluminum, then folded and connected with simple hand tools. Researchers also developed a computer-based system that calculates the shape each piece needs to take to create the final form.
Despite using relatively little material, the resulting structures can be surprisingly strong. In simulations reported in the research paper, the team’s woven design was up to 3.5 times stiffer than another configuration made from the same amount of material.
To show that the idea could work at a much larger scale, the team created Lexicon , a 23-foot-wide sculpture made from folded aluminum. A group with no professional construction experience assembled the structure in a matter of days before suspending it inside the Boston Public Library.
The same approach could eventually have uses far beyond sculpture. Because the components can be transported flat and assembled relatively quickly, researchers imagine using the system for emergency shelters, architectural facades, lightweight aerospace components, and other structures where strength and low weight matter.

Cooking content can be extremely popular on social media, but watching Toronto-area Chef Maddy Goldberg narrate her made-from-scratch recipes, it suddenly all tastes a little sweeter.
That’s because every Tuesday for years, Goldberg has been donating her time to prepare banquets for 100 people in need out of what she finds at the local food bank.
“POV cooking lunch for 100 people using the random food I find at the food bank,” reads a caption at the bottom of every video.
Far from just making spaghetti and meat sauce, or canned this with a side of canned that, Goldberg uses an arsenal of different techniques and flavors to make restaurant-quality dishes, like a lentil fritter spiced with caramelized onion, cinnamon, and curry powder.
Despite attending university for social work, it was the constant cooking for herself and her friends, coupled with an enthusiasm for the cooking competitions Chopped and Top Chef that baked a love of the culinary arts that saw her change her academic path.
Finding herself in the world of fine dining, she told TODAY , there were career characteristics that often disturbed her.
A post shared by Maddy Goldberg (@maddygoldberg)
“The main rule was, ‘Never run out of anything.’ The worst thing you could do was have to tell your chef you’re out of an ingredient, so you can’t complete a dish,” she says. “ So, we would just throw out so much food, it was insane.”
“I always wanted to volunteer at a food bank to understand the other side of the food system. What happens if instead of wasting the food, we gave it to a charity? How does that work?”
Goldberg would eventually leave the restaurant world in favor of private cheffing so as to make sure she had time and room to volunteer, which she began to do at Fort York Food Bank in Toronto.
A post shared by Maddy Goldberg (@maddygoldberg)
She told TODAY that anyone inspired by her work to help those in need don’t have to cook for 100 people. Go to your local food bank, she suggests, and ask what they need. You might find you already have it in your house somewhere—some jar of spice or a pile of food storage bags you’ve never used.
She now boasts 180,000 followers of her work on Instagram, where her food bank banquet prep videos go back to January of 2025, regularly make their mouths—and their hearts—drool.

Many of the civil rights initiatives championed by the Kennedy Administration and its successor were spearheaded by RFK, who was also known as “Bobby” .
On the night that Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed, Robert F Kennedy delivered the news to the people of Indianapolis, Indiana. Local police warned him that a riot could break out there in the heart of an African-American ghetto. He wrote his notes on the ride over and started his speech without any drafts, delivering it on the back of a Flatbed truck. Although all major US cities experienced riots, Indianapolis remained calm, thanks to RFK’s speech.
63 days after that night, RFK was assassinated at age 42 while campaigning for the Presidency. Since his death in 1968, his wife Ethel raised their 11 children and never remarried. She oversaw the Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice & Human Rights until her death last year.

It protects a mountainous region in northern Wales of the same name of 827 square miles of myth-shrouded mountains and valleys. Much of the park is undeveloped, but there are also many agricultural activities that go on.
The English name for the area derives from Snowdon, which is the highest mountain in Wales at 3,560 feet (1,090 meters). In Welsh, the area is named Eryri. A commonly held belief is that the name is derived from eryr (“eagle”), and thus means “the abode/land of eagles.”
Snowdonia is one of the wettest parts of the UK, and a part of Snowdonia is the wettest part. Nevertheless it remains well-visited by domestic tourists—3.5 million of whom come to partake in the serious hiking and mountain climbing on offer in the park.

items.desc: Campaigners call for restrictions on sewage treatment plant discharging effluent during drought
items.text:
Alice Elliott is part of the Citizen's Science Project in Peterchurch, who want restrictions on treated discharges during drought
A group of residents have said pools of treated sewage are forming on a dry riverbed that runs through their village during drought conditions.
They are calling for the Environment Agency to stop the sewage treatment plant in Peterchurch, Herefordshire, discharging into the River Dore during periods of no flow.
At the moment, Welsh Water legally discharges directly into the river, but campaigners said its permit assumed the effluent would be diluted by the river flow.
The company said the plant was operating in accordance with the permit, but it was liaising with residents over their concerns.
Locals have formed a Citizen's Science Project for the Dore catchment and say lab tests have shown the waste contains "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus" as well as harmful bacteria including "worrying amounts of E. coli".
The River Dore that feeds into the Monnow and then the Wye, has seen long periods of 'no flow' over the last 15 years
Alice Elliott from the group said they had seen periods of drought affecting the river level for several years:
"Where the river stops flowing it goes completely dry, absolutely no flow.
"The sewage treatment works is continually discharging onto a dry riverbed and it's created a large pool of treated but undiluted effluent."
The group said it had samples from the site tested in a laboratory and were seeing "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus".
"Treated effluent isn't clean sanitised water." said Elliott.
"We've noticed that it contains worrying amounts of E. coli and other bacteria that are harmful to health... Normally it would get diluted down and that's what the permit allows".

items.title: Goats drafted in to tame Greenwich Park slope
items.desc: Bagot goats are used to keep vegetation in check and help preserve the view from the Royal Observatory.
items.text:
The goats are grazing just below Flamsteed House, home of the Royal Observatory's famous red time ball
A park in south-east London has taken on some new groundskeepers, and they are more than happy to eat on the job.
A small herd of rare Bagot goats has been brought in to clear a steep, overgrown slope below the Royal Observatory in Greenwich Park, in a trial run by The Royal Parks charity.
Over five days the animals will chomp through tough, woody plants and thorny stems on Castle Hill Bank, a patch that is hard to reach with machinery or by hand.
Visitors can watch them at work until Friday, between 11:00 and 15:30 GMT.
The trial uses conservation grazing, a traditional method in which animals keep dominant vegetation in check, giving other plants room to grow and supporting wildlife.
The Royal Parks is working with Mudchute Park and Farm, on the Isle of Dogs, and the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, with funding from players of People's Postcode Lottery.
Bagots are Britain's oldest native breed of goat, according to the charity. They are small and light-footed, which makes them well suited to steep and uneven ground.
Clare Lanes, Greenwich Park manager, said the view of Flamsteed House above the bank was part of what made the park so special as a Unesco World Heritage Site.
"But it's a very steep bank, and managing vegetation to protect that view is a real challenge," she said.
"We're trialling a traditional approach by bringing in goats to graze, which we hope will help us protect the landscape more sustainably."
Holly, brambles and thorny stems are all on the menu at Castle Hill Bank
She said the approach could also help the charity in its ambition to create climate-resilient parks for future generations as well as making a few visitors smile.
The herd is kept in a paddock with a lean-to shelter and fresh water, and is shepherded on and off site each day.
The goats are being watched over by Tom Davis, farm manager at Mudchute, which has previously worked with The Royal Parks on similar projects in other London parks.
He said the scheme was giving an "incredibly rare breed" an important purpose.
Charlotte Cass, who manages The Royal Parks' Help Nature Thrive project, said the charity was "always looking for exciting ways to support nature" and new ways to manage its eight London parks.
"This project helps create a better, more viable habitat for invertebrates, birds and small mammals in Greenwich Park in the longer term," she said.

Xingzi Gu, “Untitled (Sitting by my window or Feline paradox),” 2026, Acrylic and oil on canvas, 42 x 32 in
Figures drift into hazy backgrounds in Xingzi Gu ’s paintings, where relationships remain unresolved, and memories seem to shift before our eyes. In Periphery Dreaming , a recently concluded solo exhibition at Make Room in Los Angeles, the artist showed work exploring adolescence, intimacy, and the uncertainty of becoming. Through layered paintings, Gu creates dreamlike scenes where bodies merge with their surroundings and familiar experiences take on an elusive quality.
Gu is drawn to moments that resist resolution. Her figures appear to wait for something, though it is rarely clear what that might be. “I’m drawn to transitional states, particularly adolescence, as they mark a moment when the inner world of a young person encounters the expectations from the external world,” Gu tells My Modern Met. “There is space for becoming, where identity is not yet fixed but remains open to transformation.”
This sense of possibility is central to Gu’s approach to painting. She works with thin washes of acrylic , gradually building up the surface as colors and forms shift. The process can take more than a year. During that time, an initial idea may give way to something entirely unexpected, and marks that once seemed like mistakes can become essential to the finished work.
“I think the layers are very much an expression of emotion through color, shape, and composition. Each layer reflects a particular moment in time, a certain feeling or thought I had while working on the painting,” Gu explains. She allows scenes to develop without deciding in advance where they will lead, giving the figures room to inhabit their own uncertain worlds. A relationship may never reach its turning point, and a shadowy form might never become fully recognizable. That lack of resolution is part of what makes the work compelling.
The canvas becomes a record of this evolving process. Gu describes it as a “recording machine” that holds traces of her changing emotional state. Earlier images may remain partially visible beneath newer layers, giving the paintings a sense of history. What appears on the surface is only part of the story. The viewer can glimpse what came before without ever seeing the full picture.

JoyDrops champions awards-eligible documentary shorts about joy, a counterweight to a category often dominated by tragedy. Good News Network has partnered with JoyDrops to spotlight these films and talk with the filmmakers behind them.
“Believe me, it never gets old,” Freddie Nole told GNN. “I’m serious.”
Nole is talking about the moment he meets a man walking out of prison, often someone with no one else coming to get him. He and his wife, Sue, take the man to a meal, buy him clothes, get him a phone and drive him to wherever he’s headed next. No two pickups are the same, he said, but one thing always is.
“The appreciation that these individuals express to us for just being there,” Nole said, “at a time when they’re most vulnerable.”
That work is at the heart of The Second Life of Freddie Nole , the latest film in GNN’s JoyDrops series.
Directed by Dana Nachman, the film rides along with Nole for a single day as he picks up a man leaving prison in Pennsylvania. Along the way, viewers learn that Nole knows this road personally. His full backstory comes only at the end.
Nachman, whose company, Sweet World Films, focuses on stories about repairing the world, had worked on wrongful conviction cases for years. But reentry was new to her. She and her business partner, Chelsea Matter, had a little money left over from another project and wanted a story that truly fit a short. A one-day road trip was the perfect container.
They reached out to Nole over Zoom. “Literally maybe 30 seconds of talking, I was like, oh God, this guy is special,” Nachman told GNN. “We call him movie gold. Freddie is life gold.”
She later learned that groups across the country do similar work, some just 50 miles from her home in Northern California. She’s glad she didn’t know sooner. “My ignorance got me to him, really,” she said.
Nole went to prison in 1969, when Richard Nixon was president. When he finally walked out, the only person he could count on was his wife, who had stood by him for more than 37 years.
He had sent her his clothing sizes so he wouldn’t stand out. They didn’t fit. “It was just a whole embarrassing situation for me,” he told GNN, “not so much the people, but that I was so detached from this normal society.”
Then he learned he was already in violation of his parole for not reporting in time. He spent four hours of his first night of freedom at the parole office. “My whole first day of being out was simply walking on pins and needles,” he said.

items.text:
A pub owner took advantage of the Christmas season, spending thousands on a festive light display to cheer up his town’s locals.
Christian Ogley says this year has been particularly tough for residents in the picturesque town of Knaresborough, England, as the cost of living soared.
“It has been a turbulent year for everyone in the area and across the UK to say the least, said the 34-year-old who owns Blind Jack’s pub in the historic North Yorkshire town set on cliffs above the River Nidd.
“I just wanted to do something nice to make people smile.”
So, in an attempt to spread some Christmas cheer, he’s spending around $6,000 on materials and electricity to erect the beautiful display on this two-story pub.
“So far it has seemed to have done that! We’ve had many compliments.”
With help from seven staff members and regulars, they spent the past week building and installing the design, which includes a 5-meter-tall tree as its (16-ft) centerpiece, surrounded by white lights imitating falling snow and huge red ribbons.
“To start it was just a bit of fun, but as I have been installing it so many people have been wanting to talk to me about it and have been posting it on social media.
“It has given them something positive to talk about.
Christian was inspired after visiting New York City and Ireland over the past two years and seeing the effort landlords put into their holiday displays.
He decided he would do the same at his watering hole—something which he says isn’t too common to see in the UK.
He started designing the mega Christmas project in January by sketching out initial ideas on the back of beer mats.
The dad-of-two who studied graphic design at university, even needed a cherry picker for the huge Christmas tree, made from wood and tarpaulin.
Altogether, it contains over 10,000 lights which he says costs him around £2.50 a day to run from 12 am to 12 pm.
“It is surprisingly cheaper than I thought to keep the lights on, which means I can keep them on for longer.
“The lights mean so much to me and the community, I’m trying to keep them glowing for as long as I can each day.”
Christian told SWNS news last week that he still isn’t finished yet, as he intends to install two seven-foot nutcrackers on the pavement.
He bought the pub in 2017 with his 33-year-old wife Alice Ogley, and last year it won an award for Best Beer Pub in the UK.
“Hopefully the display can become a bit of a tradition and something locals can look forward to every year.”

items.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
items.desc: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
items.text:
Will COP31 end with a new global climate deal?
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock and have been suspended for the night, after running more than a day over time, as countries have been unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.
If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.
In that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement
On Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.
"These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together."
Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

items.text:
American conservationists have secured protections for a truly unique-in-the-world ecosystem along the state’s Bering Sea coastline.
Home to the largest concentrations of Pacific walrus found anywhere in North America, the barrier islands off the coast of the tiny northern village of Point Lay provide a critical refuge for these marine megafauna.
Now ensconced within a 47,000-acre protected area (74 square miles) held by the Interior Alaska Land Trust, the islands have been spared from industrial development and other disturbances, as has “one of the largest, undiminished coastal lagoon systems in the world,” which was protected in tandem.
Part of the coalition that for 10 years has worked towards securing protections for the Point Lay barrier islands and the Kasegaluk Lagoon, The Conservation Fund explains that the islands hadn’t historically been a walrus mecca until 2007, when the animals changed their seasonal migration behavior in mass.
Every year, a quarter million Pacific walrus would migrate north through the Bering Strait, with the males remaining out at sea and the females with their calves moving towards the shallow, nutrient-rich waters of the Chukchi Sea between Alaska and Russia.
Historically, these animals relied on Arctic sea ice for resting spots, but by 2007 the ice had become inconsistent. One year, an estimated 200,000 walrus hauled themselves up onto the barrier islands of Point Lay, and they’ve returned every year ever since.
That includes every single female and juvenile Pacific walrus on Earth—all stuffed onto beaches that will now forever be theirs thanks to The Conservation Fund and its partners among the Alaska tribal nations and the Interior Alaska Land Trust.
The new conservation easement, held by the Trust, will increase monitoring and stewardship to actively minimize disturbance to walrus and other animals as commercial and tourist activity in the Alaskan Arctic continues to expand. Conservation Fund noted that encroachment from humans had already caused undesirable stampede events among the resting animals.
